question: How do Daniel and his companions come to Babylon, and what does the king do to turn them into servants of the court?
The verb גָּאַל (ga’al, “defile oneself”) explains Daniel's decision about the king's food: why could eating from that table be seen as defilement for a Jew in exile?
How does Daniel negotiate with the chief official and with the steward, and what does this way of acting show about his faithfulness?
Daniel “made up his mind” before he was pressured: in what area of your life is it worth deciding in advance how far you will go?
From verse 4 the book switches from Hebrew to Aramaic: what does Nebuchadnezzar demand of the wise men, and why do they consider the demand impossible?

The Aramaic word רָז (raz, “mystery”) appears in the friends' request, in the revelation and in Daniel's words to the king: who knows the mystery, according to the chapter, and how does it reach human beings?
What do the statue of several metals and the stone cut out “without human hands” communicate about human kingdoms and the kingdom the God of heaven will set up?
Before going to the king, Daniel gathers his friends to pray and then praises God: how do you usually act when you face a problem you do not know how to solve?
How does the chapter describe the golden statue and the ceremony of its dedication, and what words and lists are repeated?
The Aramaic verb סְגִד (segid, “bow down, worship”) is repeated in the king's order and in the three young men's refusal: what was at stake in this gesture of bowing down?
What does the phrase “But even if He does not” reveal about the trust of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in God's power and in His freedom to act?
The three were not spared the furnace, but found company within it: what does this scene say to you about trials that may not be avoided?
What does the king see in the dream of the tree, and what does the watcher order to be done with it?
The Aramaic term עִיר (‘ir, “watcher”) appears only in this chapter of the Bible: what role do these watchers have in the sentence against the king?
How does the sentence spoken on the palace roof relate to what happens next, and what changes when the king lifts his eyes to heaven?
Daniel advises the king to break off his sins by doing righteousness and showing mercy to the oppressed: what concrete form could this advice take in your life?
What happens at Belshazzar's feast, and what sacred objects are used there?
Why does Daniel recall the story of Nebuchadnezzar before interpreting the writing, and of what is Belshazzar accused?
The Aramaic word תְּקַל (teqal, “weighed”) is tied to weights and measures: what does it mean for the king to be “weighed on the scales” and found “deficient”?
Daniel refuses the gifts but reads the writing: in what situations is it hard for you to speak the truth without expecting something in return?
Why can the administrators and satraps find no fault in Daniel, and what plan do they devise?
The Aramaic verb צְלָא (tsela’, “pray”) describes Daniel's habit of praying three times a day facing Jerusalem: what does this custom show about his life in exile?
How does King Darius behave before and after throwing Daniel into the den, and what does the text suggest about the power of a king bound by his own law?
Daniel goes on praying “just as he had done before”: what practices of your faith would you keep even under pressure to abandon them?
How are the four beasts that come up out of the great sea described, and what stands out about the little horn?
The Aramaic בַּר אֱנָשׁ (bar ’enash, “son of man”) describes the one who comes with the clouds: how does this human figure contrast with the beasts from the sea, and how does Jesus use this title?
What does the scene of the Ancient of Days, with thrones, fire and open books, communicate about who has the last word in history?
The chapter is the last in Aramaic, and Daniel ends up alarmed: what different ways of identifying the kingdoms and the saints do you know, and what does the text itself leave open?
The vision promises the kingdom to “the saints of the Most High” after a time of oppression: how can this promise sustain someone who suffers for their faith?
Where does Daniel have the vision, and what do the ram, the goat and the little horn do?
The word קֶרֶן (qeren, “horn”) appears in almost the whole vision: what did the horn represent as an image of strength in the world of the Bible, and how does the angel explain some of them?
What question do the holy ones ask about the sanctuary, and what concern does it reveal about the worship of God?
Daniel goes back to the king's business but remains appalled by the vision: how do you deal with what you do not understand while carrying on with the responsibilities of daily life?
What does Daniel read in Jeremiah, and how does he react to this reading?
Why does Daniel confess the people's sins saying “we have sinned,” and on what does he base his plea in verse 18?
The word שָׁבוּעַ (shavua‘, “week, period of seven”) organizes Gabriel's answer: how is it linked to Jeremiah's seventy years, and what different readings of this passage do you know?
Daniel prays “not because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion”: on what do you usually base your prayers?
Under what circumstances does Daniel have this vision, and how is the man clothed in linen described?
The word שַׂר (sar, “prince, chief”) is used for Persia, Greece and Michael: what does this language suggest about the relationship between what happens on earth and what Daniel does not see?
Why is the answer to Daniel's prayer delayed, according to the messenger, and what does this indicate about the relationship between prayer and time?
Daniel receives strength when he hears “Do not be afraid, O man precious; peace be with you; be strong!”: what word of encouragement do you need today, or to whom could you say it?
What kind of events does the messenger announce about the king of the South and the king of the North, and what words are repeated in this account?
How does the chapter describe the king who desecrates the sanctuary and exalts himself above every god, and what different identifications of him do you know?
The verb שָׂכַל (sakhal, “be wise, have insight”) describes those who instruct many and still fall: what role do these wise ones have in a time of persecution?
“The people who know their God will firmly resist”: what difference does knowing God make when there is flattery and pressure to give in?
What will happen to Daniel's people “at that time,” and what does verse 2 say about those who sleep in the dust of the earth?
The word קֵץ (qets, “end”) appears several times in the final chapter: what end is being spoken of, and why is Daniel ordered to seal the book until that time?
Daniel says “I heard, but I did not understand”: what does this admission suggest about how to read the visions of the book?
The book ends with “But as for you, go your way until the end. You will rest”: how can this personal word guide someone who does not see all the answers?
